演奏普通響板時，通常每手持一對，繩圈套過拇指，板面貼掌，手指彎曲扶住另一側；靠手: In playing ordinary castanets you usually hold one pair in each hand, the loop over the thumb, the shell against the palm and the fingers curled around the other side; the fingers squeeze the two concave shells together. The lower pair mostly beats time with the fingers held together, while the higher pair can vary with all four fingers, and rapid strokes make a rustling sound. If the cord is elastic and tied tight the shells come back after each stroke; a plain cord has to be pulled through the loop to tighten it. Handle castanets are swung up and down at the wrist so that the shell strikes the partition, either free in the air or against the thigh for support. A castanet machine has one shell in each hand, struck on the board, and suits dense rhythms.
起源不明，但手持拍擊伴舞古希臘埃及已有；腓尼基人約三千年前地中海貿易使其傳入今西: The origin is unknown, but hand-held clappers struck to accompany dancing already existed in ancient Greece and Egypt; Phoenician traders carried them around the Mediterranean about three thousand years ago to what is now Spain, and by about 200 BC the Romans found them used there by the native peoples, after which they became an important accompaniment to folk music. In the Baroque they entered dance music, and Lully wrote them into ballets of Spanish, Egyptian and other character. In recent times handle castanets and the castanet machine appeared, used in the orchestra and in the jug band. Late Ottoman dancers used the çalpara, later replaced by small metal cymbals.

響板為手持體鳴樂器，霍恩博斯特尔–薩克斯編號111.141。主要發聲體為兩片凹形: The castanets are a hand-held idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.141. The main sounding parts are two concave shells, traditionally of hardwood, commonly chestnut, also jacaranda and rosewood; bone was used early on, and the similar instruments of ancient Egypt were of wood, ivory and metal. Today plastic, fibreglass and cheap woods are common. The shells are joined at one end by a cord, with the holes drilled towards the inside. Metal variants also exist. The source does not describe the materials of the handles, the partition or the board.
響板為體鳴樂器，發聲原理為兩片凹形板以繩相連，手指夾動使板面互擊，產生短促點擊聲: The castanets are an idiophone: two concave shells joined by a cord are squeezed together by the fingers so that the shells strike each other and make a short click; rapid repeated clicks make a tearing or rustling sound. The player usually holds one pair in each hand, the two pairs slightly different in pitch; the lower beats time with the fingers together and the higher varies with all four fingers and can make a sound like a roll. Mounting them on a handle or a board makes them easier to play but changes the timbre, especially in the castanet machine; hand-held castanets strike the partition by swinging the wrist, and the castanet machine has one shell in each hand and can play dense rhythms.
響板見於西班牙、摩爾、奧斯曼、希臘、義大利、墨西哥、塞法迪、葡萄牙、菲律賓、巴西: The castanets appear in the music of Spain, the Moors, the Ottomans, Greece, Italy, Mexico, the Sephardim, Portugal, the Philippines, Brazil and Switzerland, and they are used in Spanish dances such as the jota, the fandango, the flamenco soleares, the sevillana and the classical bolero. In orchestral and operatic scoring they appear in Bizet's Carmen, Richard Strauss's Salome, Wagner's Tannhäuser, Rimsky-Korsakov's Capriccio espagnol, Ravel's Rapsodie espagnole, Poulenc's Concerto for two pianos, Milhaud's La femme enlevée and Carl Jenkins's Tangollen.
響板（Castanets）是手持體鳴敲擊樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs: The castanets are a hand-held idiophone percussion instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.141, used in folk music in Europe, Spain and elsewhere. They are two concave plates of wood or other hard material joined at one end by a cord, and they are held in the palm or the web of the hand and clicked together with the fingers; the player usually holds one pair in each hand, the lower beating time and the higher varying. Handle types and the castanet machine also exist, for the orchestra or for rhythmic accompaniment.
